title: Task Scheduler
pattern: Greedy with a max-heap: most frequent task first
statement: A CPU must run the given `tasks` (letters), one per time slot. Two runs of the **same** task must be at least `n` slots apart; if nothing may run, the CPU stays idle for that slot. Return the smallest number of slots needed to finish everything.

example.why: One best schedule is A B idle A B idle A B — eight slots.

idea: The task with the most runs left is the bottleneck: its runs must be spread out, so it should be started as early and as often as allowed.
Work in blocks of `n + 1` slots. Inside one block each task runs at most once — that automatically keeps equal tasks `n` slots apart.

Fill each block with the tasks that have the most runs left (a max-heap gives them). A full block costs `n + 1` slots, idle ones included; only the very last block costs just the slots it actually used.

complexity.timeWhy: T = number of tasks, n = the gap. Counting takes O(T). The loop then walks every slot of every block, idle ones included, and there can be as many blocks as the most common task has runs. The heap never holds more than 26 letters, so each heap operation is effectively O(1). (A formula based only on the most common task gets the same answer in O(T).)

steps.text: Our example: **`tasks = ["A","A","A","B","B","B"], n = 2`**. Each step runs one highlighted line of the code.
Count how many times each task has to run.
From here on only the **counts** matter, not the letters. They go into a max-heap (stored as negative numbers), so the task with the most runs left is always on top.
Start a block of n + 1 = 3 slots. Within one block every task may run at most once, which keeps two runs of the same task at least 2 slots apart.
